faqs.a: Yes — there are no accounts, no timers that cut out, and no ads interrupting your practice. The Web Audio scheduler runs as long as your tab is open.
The tool measures the average gap between your last taps and converts it to BPM (60,000 ÷ average milliseconds). Tap at least twice, steadily, for a stable reading.
A lookahead scheduler plans each click about 120 ms in advance using the audio clock, which is far more precise than the screen timer. That is why it stays steady even on busy devices.
faqs.q: Why is it more accurate than a phone timer app?

faqs.a: Keep the tab open and audible. Browsers may throttle background tabs; if beats sound uneven, bring the tab to the front. Some mobile browsers pause audio when the screen locks.
faqs.q: Can I use it with the screen off?

faqs.a: Start 10–20 BPM below your target, play the passage cleanly three times, then raise by 4 BPM. The tap-tempo button helps you find the exact tempo of recordings you want to learn.
faqs.q: How should I practice with it?

faqs.a: BPM is just a speed number, so any instrument — guitar, piano, drums, violin — works the same. Set the beats-per-bar to match the time signature you are practicing.

metronome.formula:
Seconds per beat = 60 ÷ BPM
Bar duration = beats per bar × 60 ÷ BPM
Example: 120 BPM → 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 s per beat
howTo: Set the tempo: drag the BPM slider, type a number (30–240), or tap the Tap button in rhythm.
Choose beats per bar (2–12) to match your time signature — 4 for 4/4, 3 for 3/4, 6 for 6/8.
Keep Accent first beat on to hear the downbeat clearly, or turn it off for a flat pulse.
Pick a click sound (click, woodblock, beep) and set a comfortable volume.
Press Start. The beat dots light up in time; press Stop when done.
keyFacts: Tempo range 30–240 BPM with slider, number input and tap tempo.

metronome.workedExample:
Set 120 BPM in 4/4.

Seconds per beat = 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 s
Bar duration = 4 × 0.5 = 2.0 s

A 3-minute song at 120 BPM has 3 × 120 = 360 beats.

Slow practice: drop to 100 BPM → 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6 s per beat, giving your fingers 20% more time per note. Raise by 4 BPM whenever a passage feels easy — from 100 to 120 BPM is just 5 small steps.
